newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Excited Branson on countdown to world balloon epic. [CORRECTED 18:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Excited Branson on countdown to world balloon epic. [CORRECTED 18:40 GMT]

text.p: British tycoon Richard Branson, enjoying "the best experience of my life", said on Tuesday he would take off within hours from southwest Morocco in his attempt to become the first to fly around the world by balloon.

"The weather conditions are good so I am expecting to fly before 12 o'clock (1200 GMT)," Branson, in a green pilot's suit with his Virgin company logo, told reporters at a military airbase near the ancient city of Marrakesh.

"I am enjoying the best experience of my life. I am confident, I am optimistic," he said, before going with his children Sam, 11, and Holly, 15, into the cordoned-off area around the huge, white Virgin Global Challenger.
A planned dawn takeoff was delayed by the complexities of inflating the giant balloon with 1.1 million cubic feet (30,000 cubic metres) of helium and hot air.
Branson, the flamboyant 46-year-old head of the Virgin group of companies, warned of possible delay of some hours in filling the balloon late on Monday night.

But shortly after 0930 GMT on Tuesday the balloon -- as high as a 12-storey building -- was finally inflated and sealed. Half a tonne of food supplies have been put aboard the cramped capsule which has a microwave oven, three pilots' seats and two beds on the deck, plus navigation and communications equipment.
One technician said the craft's total weight would be 12 tonnes, including six huge advertising cans for Virgin drinks to be suspended from the accommodation capsule.

Co-pilot Rory McCarthy, who was to have made up the trio of balloonists with Branson and Per Lindstrand, told reporters he had to pull out because of suspected pneumonia. He was replaced by Alex Ritchie, 50, who was on standby as reserve co-pilot.
"There will be no flight like this one in future. I wish them a good flight," a disappointed McCarthy said.
The weather in Marrakesh, chosen as an ideal spot to enter the southern jet stream, was reported perfect for takeoff.
Twelve rods and three "umbilical cords" are tethering the balloon. At takeoff, the rods will be automatically disengaged, and finally the cords cut.
Nearly 195 feet (60 metres) tall, the balloon carrying the three men should soar to 30,000 feet (9,150 metres) and pass over the nearby snowcapped Atlas Mountains.
It will then head east over North Africa, Saudi Arabia, India, the South China Sea, the Pacific and then across the United States, with touchdown planned for Oxfordshire in southern England.
Branson expects the trip to take 14 to 21 days, with what he termed "a realistic time" of 18 days.
Branson is racing against American balloonist Steve Fosset planning a launch from St. Louis, Missouri, in the United States.
(Corrects Fosset's launch location from Switzerland).
"I am aware of the competition but I can assure you that we will be one or two days ahead of Steve Fosset," Branson said.
Branson had to cancel a previous attempt to circumnavigate the globe from Marrakesh last January because of bad weather.
The flamboyant entrepreneur, whose products range from condoms to cola and an airline, has already crossed the Atlantic and Pacific by balloon.
According to the Guinness Book of Records the furthest flown by a manned balloon is 8,382 km (5,208 miles), set by American Ben Abruzzo and three co-pilots in 1981 from Japan to California.
